Measurement: Eigenvalues and Expectation Values

What you need to know

  • The eigenfunctions of a Hermitian operator are a coordinate system for states. Any state can be expanded as ψ=∑ncnϕn\psi = \sum_n c_n\phi_nψ=∑n​cn​ϕn​, and each coefficient is a projection, cn=⟨ϕn∣ψ⟩c_n = \langle \phi_n \vert \psi \ranglecn​=⟨ϕn​∣ψ⟩.

  • A measurement of AAA returns one of the eigenvalues ana_nan​, never anything in between, with probability pn=∣cn∣2p_n = \lvert c_n\rvert^2pn​=∣cn​∣2. Normalization makes the probabilities add up to one.

  • The average of many readings is ⟨A⟩=∑npnan=⟨ψ∣A^∣ψ⟩\langle A \rangle = \sum_n p_n a_n = \langle \psi \vert \hat{A} \vert \psi \rangle⟨A⟩=∑n​pn​an​=⟨ψ∣A^∣ψ⟩. The spread σA\sigma_AσA​ vanishes only when the state is an eigenfunction.

  • Right after a reading of ana_nan​ the system is in ϕn\phi_nϕn​ (the state collapses), so an immediate second measurement gives ana_nan​ again.

  • Position eigenfunctions are spikes and momentum eigenfunctions are plane waves; each is a superposition of all the others. A state’s momentum components are its Fourier transform, ϕ(p)=⟨p∣ψ⟩\phi(p) = \langle p \vert \psi \rangleϕ(p)=⟨p∣ψ⟩, and a wave packet is a bundle of plane waves with nearby momenta.

  • Observables whose operators do not commute cannot both be sharp: σA σB≥12∣⟨[A^,B^]⟩∣\sigma_A\,\sigma_B \geq \tfrac{1}{2}\lvert\langle[\hat{A},\hat{B}]\rangle\rvertσA​σB​≥21​∣⟨[A^,B^]⟩∣, which for position and momentum is σx σp≥ℏ/2\sigma_x\,\sigma_p \geq \hbar/2σx​σp​≥ℏ/2.

Operators 2 showed that observables are Hermitian operators, with real eigenvalues and orthonormal eigenfunctions. This lecture is about what happens when we use one: postulates 3 and 4, what a measurement returns and how often. The map shows how the pieces connect.

Fig. How the postulates connect, in the order of these lectures. A state and a Hermitian observable give real eigenvalues, the possible readings, and orthogonal eigenfunctions, the axes. Any state is a superposition along those axes, with components cn=⟨ϕn∣ψ⟩c_n = \langle \phi_n \vert \psi\ranglecn​=⟨ϕn​∣ψ⟩. One measurement returns a single reading ana_nan​ and leaves the state in ϕn\phi_nϕn​. Repeated on many identically prepared copies, the reading ana_nan​ turns up in a fraction pn=∣cn∣2p_n = \lvert c_n\rvert^2pn​=∣cn​∣2 of them, and the readings average to ⟨A⟩\langle A\rangle⟨A⟩. Circled numbers are the postulates in the table of Operators 1. This lecture covers the two middle boxes; time evolution (5) is the subject of Time Dependence.

Eigenfunctions are a coordinate system¶

The eigenfunctions of a Hermitian operator work like the perpendicular axes of a plane. We start with a vector in a plane, then take the same two steps with a function, in the same Dirac notation: the structure is identical.

A vector: build it, then project¶

  • Take two perpendicular unit vectors ∣u1⟩\lvert u_1\rangle∣u1​⟩ and ∣u2⟩\lvert u_2\rangle∣u2​⟩: ⟨u1∣u1⟩=⟨u2∣u2⟩=1\langle u_1 \vert u_1\rangle = \langle u_2 \vert u_2\rangle = 1⟨u1​∣u1​⟩=⟨u2​∣u2​⟩=1 and ⟨u1∣u2⟩=0\langle u_1 \vert u_2\rangle = 0⟨u1​∣u2​⟩=0. Every vector in their plane is a linear combination of them:

∣v⟩=c1∣u1⟩+c2∣u2⟩\lvert v\rangle = c_1\lvert u_1\rangle + c_2\lvert u_2\rangle∣v⟩=c1​∣u1​⟩+c2​∣u2​⟩
(1)

  • To find c1c_1c1​, put the bra ⟨u1∣\langle u_1\rvert⟨u1​∣ in front of both sides. Orthonormality keeps one term, and the bra ⟨u2∣\langle u_2\rvert⟨u2​∣ gives c2c_2c2​ the same way:

⟨u1∣v⟩=c1 ⟨u1∣u1⟩⏟1+c2 ⟨u1∣u2⟩⏟0=c1\langle u_1 \vert v\rangle = c_1\,\underbrace{\langle u_1 \vert u_1\rangle}_{1} + c_2\,\underbrace{\langle u_1 \vert u_2\rangle}_{0} = c_1⟨u1​∣v⟩=c1​1⟨u1​∣u1​⟩​​+c2​0⟨u1​∣u2​⟩​​=c1​
(2)

# synced: vector_projection
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation
from IPython.display import HTML

TEAL, CARDINAL, GRAY, PURPLE, ORANGE = "#107895", "#C8102E", "#6c757d", "#6a3d9a", "#e07b00"
plt.rcParams.update({"axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})
a = np.radians(30)
u1, u2 = np.array([np.cos(a), np.sin(a)]), np.array([-np.sin(a), np.cos(a)])   # tilted perpendicular unit vectors
c1, c2 = 3.0, 1.5
v = c1 * u1 + c2 * u2
arrow = lambda ax, tail, tip, col, lw, ms, z: ax.annotate("", xy=tip, xytext=tail, zorder=z, arrowprops=dict(
    arrowstyle="-|>", color=col, lw=lw, mutation_scale=ms, shrinkA=0, shrinkB=0))
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.6, 4.3), gridspec_kw={"wspace": 0.06})
for ax in axs:
    for u in (u1, u2):                                      # the two axes, faint
        ax.plot(*np.outer([-0.75, 3.9], u).T, color=GRAY, lw=0.9, alpha=0.45, zorder=1)
    arrow(ax, (0, 0), u1, "k", 2.2, 14, 5); arrow(ax, (0, 0), u2, "k", 2.2, 14, 5)
    ax.text(*(u1 + np.array([0.0, -0.36])), r"$|u_1\rangle$", fontsize=14, ha="center")
    ax.text(*(u2 + np.array([0.14, -0.06])), r"$|u_2\rangle$", fontsize=14, ha="left")
    arrow(ax, (0, 0), v, TEAL, 3, 20, 4)
    ax.text(*(v + np.array([0.1, 0.08])), r"$|v\rangle$", color=TEAL, fontsize=17)
    ax.set_xlim(-2.5, 3.45); ax.set_ylim(-0.75, 3.3); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")
b = axs[0]                                                  # build: tip to tail
arrow(b, (0, 0), c1 * u1, PURPLE, 2.8, 18, 3)
arrow(b, c1 * u1, v, ORANGE, 2.8, 18, 3)
b.text(*(0.62 * c1 * u1 + np.array([0.28, -0.42])), r"$c_1|u_1\rangle$", color=PURPLE, fontsize=15, ha="center")
b.text(*(c1 * u1 + 0.55 * c2 * u2 + np.array([0.2, 0.0])), r"$c_2|u_2\rangle$", color=ORANGE, fontsize=15, ha="left")
b.set_title(r"build:  $|v\rangle = c_1|u_1\rangle + c_2|u_2\rangle$", loc="left", fontsize=14)
q = axs[1]                                                  # project: drop perpendiculars onto each axis
p1, p2 = c1 * u1, c2 * u2
q.plot(*np.array([v, p1]).T, color=PURPLE, ls="--", lw=1.5, zorder=2)
q.plot(*np.array([v, p2]).T, color=ORANGE, ls="--", lw=1.5, zorder=2)
q.plot(*np.array([[0, 0], p1]).T, color=PURPLE, lw=7, alpha=0.5, solid_capstyle="butt", zorder=2)
q.plot(*np.array([[0, 0], p2]).T, color=ORANGE, lw=7, alpha=0.5, solid_capstyle="butt", zorder=2)
for foot, along, up in ((p1, u1, u2), (p2, u2, u1)):        # right-angle marks at the feet
    sq = np.array([foot - 0.17 * along, foot - 0.17 * along + 0.17 * up, foot + 0.17 * up])
    q.plot(*sq.T, color=GRAY, lw=1.1, zorder=2)
q.text(*(0.45 * p1 + 0.55 * (-u2)), r"$c_1 = \langle u_1|v\rangle = 3$", color=PURPLE, fontsize=15, ha="left", va="center")
q.text(*(0.75 * p2 + 0.3 * (-u1)), r"$c_2 = \langle u_2|v\rangle$" + "\n" + r"$= 1.5$", color=ORANGE, fontsize=15, ha="right", va="center")
q.set_title(r"project:  $c_k = \langle u_k|v\rangle$, the shadow on axis $k$", loc="left", fontsize=14)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.01, right=0.99, top=0.9, bottom=0.02)
plt.show()

Fig. Left: the vector ∣v⟩\lvert v\rangle∣v⟩ built from c1∣u1⟩c_1\lvert u_1\ranglec1​∣u1​⟩ and c2∣u2⟩c_2\lvert u_2\ranglec2​∣u2​⟩, tip to tail. Right: the same coefficients found by projection; each ck=⟨uk∣v⟩c_k = \langle u_k \vert v\rangleck​=⟨uk​∣v⟩ is the shadow of ∣v⟩\lvert v\rangle∣v⟩ on its own axis. Here c1=3c_1 = 3c1​=3 and c2=1.5c_2 = 1.5c2​=1.5.

A function: the same two steps¶

  • A wavefunction in a box is built the same way, with the box states ∣ψn⟩\lvert\psi_n\rangle∣ψn​⟩, ψn=2/L sin⁡(nπx/L)\psi_n = \sqrt{2/L}\,\sin(n\pi x/L)ψn​=2/L​sin(nπx/L), in place of the unit vectors. They are orthonormal, ⟨ψm∣ψn⟩=δmn\langle \psi_m \vert \psi_n\rangle = \delta_{mn}⟨ψm​∣ψn​⟩=δmn​, and there are enough of them to build any state in the box:

∣ψ⟩=c1∣ψ1⟩+c2∣ψ2⟩+c3∣ψ3⟩+⋯\lvert\psi\rangle = c_1\lvert\psi_1\rangle + c_2\lvert\psi_2\rangle + c_3\lvert\psi_3\rangle + \cdots∣ψ⟩=c1​∣ψ1​⟩+c2​∣ψ2​⟩+c3​∣ψ3​⟩+⋯
(3)

  • The bra ⟨ψm∣\langle \psi_m\rvert⟨ψm​∣ picks out one coefficient, exactly as for the vector. The only new step is how to compute a bracket of two functions: multiply them point by point and integrate.

⟨ψm∣ψ⟩=∑ncn ⟨ψm∣ψn⟩⏟δmn=cm,⟨ψm∣ψ⟩=∫0Lψm∗ ψ dx\langle \psi_m \vert \psi\rangle = \sum_n c_n\,\underbrace{\langle \psi_m \vert \psi_n\rangle}_{\delta_{mn}} = c_m, \qquad \langle \psi_m \vert \psi\rangle = \int_0^L \psi_m^*\,\psi\,dx⟨ψm​∣ψ⟩=n∑​cn​δmn​⟨ψm​∣ψn​⟩​​=cm​,⟨ψm​∣ψ⟩=∫0L​ψm∗​ψdx
(4)

# synced: function_projection
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation
from IPython.display import HTML

TEAL, CARDINAL, GRAY, PURPLE, ORANGE = "#107895", "#C8102E", "#6c757d", "#6a3d9a", "#e07b00"
plt.rcParams.update({"axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})
x = np.linspace(0, 1, 400)
psi = np.sqrt(30) * x * (1 - x)                             # the state of the worked example, L = 1
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.6, 3.5), gridspec_kw={"wspace": 0.1})
for ax, n in zip(axs, (1, 3)):                              # n = 2 is zero by symmetry (see the Example)
    phi = np.sqrt(2) * np.sin(n * np.pi * x)
    prod = phi * psi
    c = np.trapezoid(prod, x)
    ax.fill_between(x, prod, where=prod >= 0, color=PURPLE, alpha=0.25, lw=0, interpolate=True)
    ax.fill_between(x, prod, where=prod < 0, color=ORANGE, alpha=0.3, lw=0, interpolate=True)
    ax.plot(x, psi, color=TEAL, lw=2.4, label=r"the state $\psi$")
    ax.plot(x, phi, color=GRAY, lw=1.6, ls="--", label=r"box state $\psi_n$")
    ax.plot(x, prod, color=PURPLE, lw=1.2, label=r"product $\psi_n\,\psi$")
    ax.axhline(0, color=GRAY, lw=0.6)
    ax.set_xlim(0, 1); ax.set_ylim(-2.2, 2.35); ax.set_yticks([])
    ax.set_xticks([0, 0.5, 1]); ax.set_xticklabels(["0", "L/2", "L"], fontsize=11)
    ax.spines["left"].set_visible(False)
    ax.set_title(rf"$c_1 = \langle\psi_1|\psi\rangle = \int\psi_1\,\psi\,dx = {c:.3f}$" if n == 1
                 else rf"$c_3 = \langle\psi_3|\psi\rangle = {c:.3f}$: the lobes nearly cancel", loc="left", fontsize=13)
axs[1].legend(loc="lower left", frameon=False, fontsize=11, handlelength=1.6, borderaxespad=0.1)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.01, right=0.99, top=0.88, bottom=0.1)
plt.show()

Each coefficient cn=⟨ψn∣ψ⟩c_n = \langle \psi_n \vert \psi\ranglecn​=⟨ψn​∣ψ⟩ is the area under the product ψnψ\psi_n\psiψn​ψ, purple where it is positive and orange where it is negative.   • How large is 0.999? Squared components add up to the length squared, for the arrow (c12+c22=32+1.52=⟨v∣v⟩c_1^2 + c_2^2 = 3^2 + 1.5^2 = \langle v \vert v\ranglec12​+c22​=32+1.52=⟨v∣v⟩) and for the function (∑n∣cn∣2=⟨ψ∣ψ⟩\sum_n \lvert c_n\rvert^2 = \langle \psi \vert \psi\rangle∑n​∣cn​∣2=⟨ψ∣ψ⟩, shown below). A normalized state has length 1, so no coefficient can exceed 1 in size, and c1=1c_1 = 1c1​=1 would mean ψ=ψ1\psi = \psi_1ψ=ψ1​. Here ∣c1∣2=0.9986\lvert c_1\rvert^2 = 0.9986∣c1​∣2=0.9986 leaves only 0.0014 for all the other box states together: the parabola is almost exactly the ground state, which is why the two curves in the left panel nearly coincide.

  • The box states are one set of axes. The eigenfunctions ϕn\phi_nϕn​ of any Hermitian operator are orthonormal and complete (Operators 2), so every state can be expanded in them:

Expansion in eigenfunctions
∣ψ⟩=∑ncn ∣ϕn⟩,cn=⟨ϕn∣ψ⟩=∫ϕn∗ ψ dx\lvert\psi\rangle = \sum_n c_n\,\lvert\phi_n\rangle, \qquad c_n = \langle \phi_n \vert \psi \rangle = \int \phi_n^*\,\psi\,dx∣ψ⟩=n∑​cn​∣ϕn​⟩,cn​=⟨ϕn​∣ψ⟩=∫ϕn∗​ψdx
(5)
Example: how much ground state is in a parabola?

The state ψ=30/L5  x(L−x)\psi = \sqrt{30/L^5}\;x(L-x)ψ=30/L5​x(L−x) vanishes at both walls, so it is a legitimate particle-in-a-box state. Expand it in the box states ψn=2/L sin⁡(nπx/L)\psi_n = \sqrt{2/L}\,\sin(n\pi x/L)ψn​=2/L​sin(nπx/L). Two integrations by parts give

cn=∫0Lψn ψ dx=60L3∫0Lx(L−x)sin⁡nπxL dx=60L3⋅2L3[1−(−1)n](nπ)3c_n = \int_0^L \psi_n\,\psi\,dx = \frac{\sqrt{60}}{L^3}\int_0^L x(L-x)\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}\,dx = \frac{\sqrt{60}}{L^3}\cdot\frac{2L^3\big[1-(-1)^n\big]}{(n\pi)^3}cn​=∫0L​ψn​ψdx=L360​​∫0L​x(L−x)sinLnπx​dx=L360​​⋅(nπ)32L3[1−(−1)n]​
(6)
cn=815(nπ)3  (n odd),cn=0  (n even)c_n = \frac{8\sqrt{15}}{(n\pi)^3}\ \ (n \text{ odd}), \qquad c_n = 0\ \ (n \text{ even})cn​=(nπ)3815​​  (n odd),cn​=0  (n even)
(7)

The even coefficients vanish by symmetry: the parabola is even about the center of the box and the even-nnn states are odd. The first few probabilities are

∣c1∣2=960π6=0.9986,∣c3∣2=960729 π6=0.0014,∣c5∣2=0.0001\lvert c_1\rvert^2 = \frac{960}{\pi^6} = 0.9986, \qquad \lvert c_3\rvert^2 = \frac{960}{729\,\pi^6} = 0.0014, \qquad \lvert c_5\rvert^2 = 0.0001∣c1​∣2=π6960​=0.9986,∣c3​∣2=729π6960​=0.0014,∣c5​∣2=0.0001
(8)

The parabola is 99.86 percent ground state, and c3=815/(3π)3=0.037c_3 = 8\sqrt{15}/(3\pi)^3 = 0.037c3​=815​/(3π)3=0.037 is the small coefficient in the right panel of the figure above.

  • A smooth, spread-out state needs few eigenfunctions. A narrow one needs many, because it takes short wavelengths, high nnn, to build a sharp feature:

# synced: sine_series
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation

TEAL, CARDINAL, GRAY, PURPLE, ORANGE = "#107895", "#C8102E", "#6c757d", "#6a3d9a", "#e07b00"

x = np.linspace(0, 1, 600)
psi = np.exp(-(x - 0.3)**2 / (4 * 0.045**2))               # |psi|^2 has width 0.045 L
psi = psi / np.sqrt(np.trapezoid(psi**2, x))
ns = np.arange(1, 31)
phis = np.sqrt(2) * np.sin(np.outer(ns, np.pi * x))
c = np.trapezoid(phis * psi, x, axis=1)
ks = np.concatenate([np.arange(1, 25), np.full(6, 24)])
fig, (ax, axb) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(8, 4.4), gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [1.5, 1], "hspace": 0.55})
ax.plot(x, psi, color="k", lw=1.4, ls=":", label=r"the state $\psi$")

band = [ax.fill_between(x, 0 * x, color=TEAL, alpha=0.15, lw=0)]
ax.axhline(0, color=GRAY, lw=0.6)
ax.set_xlim(0, 1); ax.set_ylim(-1.6, 3.6); ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_xticks([0, 0.5, 1]); ax.set_xticklabels(["0", "L/2", "L"], fontsize=12)

bars = axb.bar(ns, c**2, color="#d9dde1", width=0.75)

axb.set_xlabel(r"$n$", fontsize=12); axb.set_ylabel(r"$|c_n|^2$", fontsize=12)

fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.08, right=0.98, top=0.9, bottom=0.12)

def update(i):
    k = ks[i]
    s = c[:k] @ phis[:k]
    part.set_data(x, s)
    band[0].remove(); band[0] = ax.fill_between(x, s, color=TEAL, alpha=0.15, lw=0)
    for j, b in enumerate(bars):
        b.set_color(TEAL if j < k else "#d9dde1")
    ax.set_title(rf"$k = {k}$ box states", loc="left", fontsize=13)
    axb.set_title(f"the first {k} states hold probability {np.sum(c[:k]**2):.3f}", loc="left", fontsize=12.5)

ani = FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=len(ks), interval=140, blit=False)

A measurement returns an eigenvalue¶

Measurement outcomes and their probabilities

A measurement of AAA on the state ψ=∑ncnϕn\psi = \sum_n c_n\phi_nψ=∑n​cn​ϕn​ returns one of the eigenvalues ana_nan​, with probability

pn=∣cn∣2=∣⟨ϕn∣ψ⟩∣2,∑npn=1p_n = \lvert c_n\rvert^2 = \big\lvert\langle \phi_n \vert \psi \rangle\big\rvert^2, \qquad \sum_n p_n = 1pn​=∣cn​∣2=∣∣​⟨ϕn​∣ψ⟩∣∣​2,n∑​pn​=1
(9)

  • The probabilities add up to one because the state is normalized. Expand both sides of ⟨ψ∣ψ⟩=1\langle \psi \vert \psi \rangle = 1⟨ψ∣ψ⟩=1; orthonormality removes every cross term:

⟨ψ∣ψ⟩=∑m∑ncm∗ cn ⟨ϕm∣ϕn⟩=∑n∣cn∣2=1\langle \psi \vert \psi \rangle = \sum_m\sum_n c_m^*\,c_n\,\langle \phi_m \vert \phi_n \rangle = \sum_n \lvert c_n\rvert^2 = 1⟨ψ∣ψ⟩=m∑​n∑​cm∗​cn​⟨ϕm​∣ϕn​⟩=n∑​∣cn​∣2=1
(10)

  • Only the size of each coefficient matters for these probabilities. The coefficients cnc_ncn​ and cneiθc_n e^{i\theta}cn​eiθ give the same pnp_npn​; the phases come back in Time Dependence.

  • A measurement does not reveal ψ\psiψ. It returns one number, and it changes the state (below). The probabilities show up only in the statistics of many identically prepared copies: many boxes, each holding one particle prepared in the same state ψ\psiψ, each measured once. Measuring one particle over and over does not work, because the first reading changes its state. It is the same story as the single detections that built up the pattern ∣ψ(x)∣2\lvert\psi(x)\rvert^2∣ψ(x)∣2 in The Schrödinger Equation. Chemistry gets its copies for free: a spectrum is recorded on a sample of something like 1020 molecules, and each molecule contributes its own reading.

Try it: pick a state and press +1 box a few times. Each press prepares a fresh box in that state and measures its energy once; after a single reading, measure it again reads the same box a second time. Then add a thousand boxes. Every reading is one of the energies En=n2E1E_n = n^2E_1En​=n2E1​ of the box, never anything in between. The bars approach ∣cn∣2\lvert c_n\rvert^2∣cn​∣2 and the running mean approaches a value we compute next.

Averages and spreads¶

  • If the reading ana_nan​ comes up with probability pnp_npn​, the average over many readings is the weighted sum ∑npnan\sum_n p_n a_n∑n​pn​an​. The integral formula of The Schrödinger Equation gives the same number. Expand ψ\psiψ and let A^\hat{A}A^ act on each eigenfunction:

⟨ψ∣A^∣ψ⟩=∑m∑ncm∗ cn ⟨ϕm∣A^∣ϕn⟩=∑m∑ncm∗ cn an δmn=∑n∣cn∣2 an\langle \psi \vert \hat{A} \vert \psi \rangle = \sum_m\sum_n c_m^*\,c_n\,\langle \phi_m \vert \hat{A} \vert \phi_n \rangle = \sum_m\sum_n c_m^*\,c_n\,a_n\,\delta_{mn} = \sum_n \lvert c_n\rvert^2\,a_n⟨ψ∣A^∣ψ⟩=m∑​n∑​cm∗​cn​⟨ϕm​∣A^∣ϕn​⟩=m∑​n∑​cm∗​cn​an​δmn​=n∑​∣cn​∣2an​
(11)
Expectation value and spread
⟨A⟩=∑npn an=⟨ψ∣A^∣ψ⟩\langle A \rangle = \sum_n p_n\,a_n = \langle \psi \vert \hat{A} \vert \psi \rangle⟨A⟩=n∑​pn​an​=⟨ψ∣A^∣ψ⟩
(12)
σA2=⟨A2⟩−⟨A⟩2=∑npn (an−⟨A⟩)2\sigma_A^2 = \langle A^2 \rangle - \langle A \rangle^2 = \sum_n p_n\,\big(a_n - \langle A \rangle\big)^2σA2​=⟨A2⟩−⟨A⟩2=n∑​pn​(an​−⟨A⟩)2
(13)

  • The spread is a sum of squares weighted by probabilities, so it vanishes only when all the probability sits on one eigenvalue: only an eigenfunction gives a sharp value.

Example: energy readings of a superposition

A particle in a box is in the state ψ=12ψ1+12ψ2+12ψ3\psi = \tfrac{1}{2}\psi_1 + \tfrac{1}{2}\psi_2 + \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\psi_3ψ=21​ψ1​+21​ψ2​+2​1​ψ3​, the default state of the widget. What readings are possible, how often, and what are their average and spread?

The readings are E1E_1E1​, 4E14E_14E1​ and 9E19E_19E1​, with probabilities 14\tfrac{1}{4}41​, 14\tfrac{1}{4}41​ and 12\tfrac{1}{2}21​, which add up to one. Then

⟨E⟩=14E1+14⋅4E1+12⋅9E1=234E1=5.75 E1\langle E \rangle = \tfrac{1}{4}E_1 + \tfrac{1}{4}\cdot4E_1 + \tfrac{1}{2}\cdot9E_1 = \tfrac{23}{4}E_1 = 5.75\,E_1⟨E⟩=41​E1​+41​⋅4E1​+21​⋅9E1​=423​E1​=5.75E1​
(14)
⟨E2⟩=14E12+14⋅16E12+12⋅81E12=44.75 E12,σE=44.75−5.752  E1=3.42 E1\langle E^2 \rangle = \tfrac{1}{4}E_1^2 + \tfrac{1}{4}\cdot16E_1^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}\cdot81E_1^2 = 44.75\,E_1^2, \qquad \sigma_E = \sqrt{44.75 - 5.75^2}\;E_1 = 3.42\,E_1⟨E2⟩=41​E12​+41​⋅16E12​+21​⋅81E12​=44.75E12​,σE​=44.75−5.752​E1​=3.42E1​
(15)

The average, 5.75 E15.75\,E_15.75E1​, is not one of the possible readings. No single measurement ever returns it.

  • The two routes to ⟨E⟩\langle E \rangle⟨E⟩, the sum over probabilities and the integral, are worth checking numerically. On a grid the box states are the eigenvectors of the Hamiltonian matrix, and the expansion coefficients are dot products:

import numpy as np

N = 1000                                          # interior points of a box with L = 1
x = np.linspace(0, 1, N + 2)[1:-1]; dx = x[1] - x[0]
H = (2 * np.eye(N) - np.eye(N, k=1) - np.eye(N, k=-1)) / (2 * dx**2)   # hbar = m = 1, V = 0
E, phi = np.linalg.eigh(H)
phi = phi / np.sqrt(dx)                           # columns normalized as functions
E1 = np.pi**2 / 2                                 # exact ground-state energy

psi = np.sqrt(30) * x * (1 - x)                   # the parabola of the example
c = phi.T @ psi * dx                              # c_n = <phi_n|psi>
p = c**2

print("p_1, p_2, p_3:", np.round(p[:3], 5))
print("sum of p_n:", round(p.sum(), 6))
print("<E> = sum p_n E_n:", round(p @ E / E1, 4), "E1")
print("<E> = <psi|H|psi>:", round(psi @ H @ psi * dx / E1, 4), "E1   (exact: 10/pi^2 =", round(10 / np.pi**2, 4), "E1)")
p_1, p_2, p_3: [0.99856 0.      0.00137]
sum of p_n: 1.0
<E> = sum p_n E_n: 1.0132 E1
<E> = <psi|H|psi>: 1.0132 E1   (exact: 10/pi^2 = 1.0132 E1)

  • The grid agrees with the exact coefficients of the example, and both routes give ⟨E⟩=10E1/π2=1.013 E1\langle E \rangle = 10E_1/\pi^2 = 1.013\,E_1⟨E⟩=10E1​/π2=1.013E1​: the parabola costs only 1.3 percent more energy than the ground state.

probability of ana_nan​∣cn∣2\lvert c_n\rvert^2∣cn​∣2∣⟨ϕn∣ψ⟩∣2\lvert\langle \phi_n \vert \psi \rangle\rvert^2∣⟨ϕn​∣ψ⟩∣2p = np.abs(c)**2

After the measurement¶

Collapse

If a measurement of AAA returns ana_nan​, the system is left in the eigenfunction ϕn\phi_nϕn​. An immediate second measurement of AAA returns ana_nan​ again, with certainty.

  • Orthogonal eigenfunctions are mutually exclusive outcomes: a system found in ϕ1\phi_1ϕ1​ has zero overlap with ϕ2\phi_2ϕ2​. A single copy never returns a mixture of readings; the mixture lives in the statistics of many copies.

  • What happens physically during the collapse is the oldest open question of quantum mechanics. The Copenhagen interpretation, worked out by Bohr and Heisenberg in the 1920s and the one most often taught, holds that a system has no definite value of AAA before it is measured; the theory predicts only the probabilities, and the measurement produces one outcome. Schrödinger found this absurd and made his point with a cat:

Compatible and incompatible observables¶

  • If [A^,B^]=0[\hat{A},\hat{B}] = 0[A^,B^]=0, the two operators share eigenfunctions (Operators 2). A reading of ana_nan​ leaves the system in a shared eigenfunction, so BBB is sharp too, and measuring BBB does not disturb the value of AAA. Such observables are compatible: energy and momentum of a free particle, or H^\hat{H}H^, L^2\hat{L}^2L^2 and L^z\hat{L}_zL^z​ for hydrogen.

  • If they do not commute, they have no complete set of eigenfunctions in common. Then an eigenfunction of one is a superposition of many eigenfunctions of the other, and a state with a sharp value of one has a spread in the other. Position and momentum, with [x^,p^]=iℏ[\hat{x},\hat{p}] = i\hbar[x^,p^​]=iℏ, are the cleanest case.

Position and momentum: spikes and plane waves¶

  • The eigenfunctions of momentum are the plane waves of Operators 2, p^ eipx/ℏ=p eipx/ℏ\hat{p}\,e^{ipx/\hbar} = p\,e^{ipx/\hbar}p^​eipx/ℏ=peipx/ℏ. Each has one momentum, and ∣eipx/ℏ∣2=1\lvert e^{ipx/\hbar}\rvert^2 = 1∣eipx/ℏ∣2=1 is the same everywhere: a plane wave is spread evenly over all positions.

  • The eigenfunctions of position are spikes. A function that vanishes everywhere except at x0x_0x0​ satisfies x ψ(x)=x0 ψ(x)x\,\psi(x) = x_0\,\psi(x)xψ(x)=x0​ψ(x), because the factor xxx only matters where ψ\psiψ is nonzero. The ideal spike, infinitely narrow with area 1, is the delta function δ(x−x0)\delta(x - x_0)δ(x−x0​) of Appendix A.6. On a grid it is easier: x^\hat{x}x^ is the diagonal matrix of Operators 1, and its eigenvectors are the columns with a single 1, one grid point each.

operatoreigenfunctionssharp valuespread over
x^\hat{x}x^spikes δ(x−x0)\delta(x - x_0)δ(x−x0​)position x0x_0x0​every momentum
p^\hat{p}p^​plane waves eipx/ℏe^{ipx/\hbar}eipx/ℏmomentum pppevery position

  • Each set is built from the other. A spike is a sum of plane waves of every momentum, all with the same weight, which add up at one point and cancel everywhere else. A plane wave is a sum of spikes at every position, all of the same size:

K, dp = 30, 0.25                                            # momenta -K dp ... K dp, equal weights

    fig.text(0.27 + 0.485 * j, 0.965, head, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=14, weight="bold", color=col)
    fig.text(0.27 + 0.485 * j, 0.5, "add them up", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=11, color=GRAY, style="italic")

Right: spikes at every grid point, each weighted by the value of eip0x/ℏe^{ip_0x/\hbar}eip0​x/ℏ there, add up to a plane wave, a sharp momentum.

  • So any state can be written either way. Write ∣x0⟩\lvert x_0 \rangle∣x0​⟩ for the spike at x0x_0x0​ and ∣p⟩\lvert p \rangle∣p⟩ for the plane wave eipx/ℏ/2πℏe^{ipx/\hbar}/\sqrt{2\pi\hbar}eipx/ℏ/2πℏ​. In the spikes, the components of ψ\psiψ are simply its values, ψ(x0)=⟨x0∣ψ⟩\psi(x_0) = \langle x_0 \vert \psi \rangleψ(x0​)=⟨x0​∣ψ⟩: the wavefunction we have drawn all along is the expansion in position eigenfunctions, just as the column of samples was on the grid.

  • In the plane waves, ψ\psiψ is a sum of many momenta, ψ(x)=∑kck eipkx/ℏ\psi(x) = \sum_k c_k\,e^{ip_kx/\hbar}ψ(x)=∑k​ck​eipk​x/ℏ. Momentum can take any value, not just a list of them, so the sum becomes an integral over ppp and the coefficients ckc_kck​ become a function ϕ(p)\phi(p)ϕ(p). Each coefficient is still a projection, as for the box states, cn=⟨ψn∣ψ⟩c_n = \langle \psi_n \vert \psi \ranglecn​=⟨ψn​∣ψ⟩. This pair of integrals is the Fourier transform:

Expansion in momentum eigenfunctions
ψ(x)=∫−∞∞ϕ(p) eipx/ℏ2πℏ dp,ϕ(p)=⟨p∣ψ⟩=∫−∞∞e−ipx/ℏ2πℏ ψ(x) dx\psi(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \phi(p)\,\frac{e^{ipx/\hbar}}{\sqrt{2\pi\hbar}}\,dp, \qquad \phi(p) = \langle p \vert \psi \rangle = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{e^{-ipx/\hbar}}{\sqrt{2\pi\hbar}}\,\psi(x)\,dxψ(x)=∫−∞∞​ϕ(p)2πℏ​eipx/ℏ​dp,ϕ(p)=⟨p∣ψ⟩=∫−∞∞​2πℏ​e−ipx/ℏ​ψ(x)dx
(16)

A momentum reading falls between ppp and p+dpp + dpp+dp with probability ∣ϕ(p)∣2 dp\lvert\phi(p)\rvert^2\,dp∣ϕ(p)∣2dp.

  • ϕ(p)\phi(p)ϕ(p) is the momentum wavefunction: the same state, written in the other coordinate system. The factor 1/2πℏ1/\sqrt{2\pi\hbar}1/2πℏ​ makes ∫∣ϕ∣2 dp=∫∣ψ∣2 dx=1\int\lvert\phi\rvert^2\,dp = \int\lvert\psi\rvert^2\,dx = 1∫∣ϕ∣2dp=∫∣ψ∣2dx=1.

Example: a Gaussian in both pictures

Take a Gaussian centered at x=0x = 0x=0, with average momentum p0p_0p0​ and position spread σx\sigma_xσx​:

ψ(x)=1(2πσx2)1/4 e−x2/4σx2 eip0x/ℏ⟹ϕ(p)=1(2πσp2)1/4 e−(p−p0)2/4σp2,σp=ℏ2σx\psi(x) = \frac{1}{(2\pi\sigma_x^2)^{1/4}}\,e^{-x^2/4\sigma_x^2}\,e^{ip_0x/\hbar} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \phi(p) = \frac{1}{(2\pi\sigma_p^2)^{1/4}}\,e^{-(p - p_0)^2/4\sigma_p^2}, \qquad \sigma_p = \frac{\hbar}{2\sigma_x}ψ(x)=(2πσx2​)1/41​e−x2/4σx2​eip0​x/ℏ⟹ϕ(p)=(2πσp2​)1/41​e−(p−p0​)2/4σp2​,σp​=2σx​ℏ​
(17)

The momentum wavefunction is again a Gaussian, centered at p0p_0p0​. Its width is inversely proportional to the position width: a packet narrow in xxx is wide in ppp, and σxσp=ℏ/2\sigma_x\sigma_p = \hbar/2σx​σp​=ℏ/2 whatever σx\sigma_xσx​ is.

Derivation: complete the square

Put ψ\psiψ into the integral for ϕ(p)\phi(p)ϕ(p) and combine the exponents. With q=(p0−p)/ℏq = (p_0 - p)/\hbarq=(p0​−p)/ℏ,

−x24σx2+iqx=−(x−2iσx2q)24σx2−σx2q2-\frac{x^2}{4\sigma_x^2} + iqx = -\frac{\big(x - 2i\sigma_x^2q\big)^2}{4\sigma_x^2} - \sigma_x^2q^2−4σx2​x2​+iqx=−4σx2​(x−2iσx2​q)2​−σx2​q2
(18)

The shifted Gaussian integrates to ∫e−(x−a)2/4σx2 dx=2σxπ\int e^{-(x - a)^2/4\sigma_x^2}\,dx = 2\sigma_x\sqrt{\pi}∫e−(x−a)2/4σx2​dx=2σx​π​, so ϕ(p)∝e−σx2(p−p0)2/ℏ2\phi(p) \propto e^{-\sigma_x^2(p - p_0)^2/\hbar^2}ϕ(p)∝e−σx2​(p−p0​)2/ℏ2. That is the Gaussian above with 1/4σp2=σx2/ℏ21/4\sigma_p^2 = \sigma_x^2/\hbar^21/4σp2​=σx2​/ℏ2, and the constants in front work out to its normalization.

  • Now squeeze and widen the Gaussian, and watch which plane waves it is made of:

Fig. A Gaussian built from plane waves. Drag the slider to squeeze or widen it. Top left: seven of the plane waves, each drawn with its weight; all of them crest together at x=0x = 0x=0. Below them: the sum over all momenta, the Gaussian itself. Right: the weights ∣ϕ(p)∣2\lvert\phi(p)\rvert^2∣ϕ(p)∣2, with the seven waves marked in matching colours. Wide in position, the packet holds a narrow band of momenta and is nearly one plane wave. Squeezed, it needs a wide band: waves of very different wavelength agree only near x=0x = 0x=0 and cancel everywhere else.

  • Squeeze the Gaussian, σx→0\sigma_x \to 0σx​→0: it becomes a spike, an eigenfunction of x^\hat{x}x^, and ϕ(p)\phi(p)ϕ(p) flattens. A sharp position holds every momentum, with equal weight.

  • Widen it, σx→∞\sigma_x \to \inftyσx​→∞: it becomes the plane wave eip0x/ℏe^{ip_0x/\hbar}eip0​x/ℏ, an eigenfunction of p^\hat{p}p^​, and ϕ(p)\phi(p)ϕ(p) collapses onto p0p_0p0​. A sharp momentum is spread over every position.

  • Neither limit is a normalizable state: a plane wave never ends, and a spike is infinitely tall. A real particle is always in between, a wave packet: a bundle of plane waves with momenta near p0p_0p0​ that add up near the center and cancel elsewhere. This is the packet promised in Waves, and the one that tunnels through barriers in Tunneling and spreads as it flies in Time Dependence. Its ∣ϕ(p)∣2\lvert\phi(p)\rvert^2∣ϕ(p)∣2 gives the momentum readings, and its center moves at p0/mp_0/mp0​/m.

Energy and momentum in a box¶

  • In a box, H^\hat{H}H^ and p^\hat{p}p^​ share no eigenfunctions either: the plane waves eipx/ℏe^{ipx/\hbar}eipx/ℏ do not vanish at the walls. Compare two states, each with its energy and momentum readings. A box state has a sharp energy; a Gaussian packet has a definite direction of motion:

Source
# synced: box_momentum
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation
from IPython.display import HTML

TEAL, CARDINAL, GRAY, PURPLE, ORANGE = "#107895", "#C8102E", "#6c757d", "#6a3d9a", "#e07b00"
plt.rcParams.update({"axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})
x = np.linspace(0, 1, 2000)                                 # L = hbar = 1: p in units of pi hbar / L
p = np.linspace(-10, 10, 1000)
kern = np.exp(-1j * np.outer(p * np.pi, x)) / np.sqrt(2 * np.pi)
ns = np.arange(1, 11)
phis = np.sqrt(2) * np.sin(np.outer(ns, np.pi * x))
packet = np.exp(-(x - 0.5)**2 / (4 * 0.1**2)) * np.exp(1j * 5 * np.pi * x)   # |psi|^2 of width 0.1 L, p0 = 5 pi hbar / L
packet = packet / np.sqrt(np.trapezoid(np.abs(packet)**2, x))
rows = [(phis[4].astype(complex), r"box state $\psi_5$", r"energy: one value, sharp", "momentum: two humps, not sharp"),
        (packet, "Gaussian packet, moving right", "energy: many values, spread", "momentum: one hump, moving right")]
fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(10, 4.9), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1, 0.85, 1.1], "hspace": 0.62, "wspace": 0.22})
for r, (psi, name, e_note, p_note) in enumerate(rows):
    axs_, axe, axp = axs[r]
    dens = np.abs(psi)**2
    axs_.fill_between(x, dens, color=CARDINAL, alpha=0.16, lw=0); axs_.plot(x, dens, color=CARDINAL, lw=1.4)
    axs_.plot(x, psi.real, color=TEAL, lw=2.2, label=r"Re $\psi$")
    axs_.axhline(0, color=GRAY, lw=0.6)
    axs_.set_xlim(0, 1); axs_.set_ylim(-2.3, 4.4); axs_.set_yticks([]); axs_.spines["left"].set_visible(False)
    axs_.set_xticks([0, 0.5, 1]); axs_.set_xticklabels(["0", "L/2", "L"], fontsize=11)
    axs_.set_title(name, loc="left", fontsize=12.5)
    c2 = np.abs(np.trapezoid(phis * psi, x, axis=1))**2
    axe.bar(ns, c2, color=PURPLE, width=0.7)
    axe.set_xlim(0.3, 10.7); axe.set_ylim(0, 1.12); axe.set_yticks([0, 0.5, 1]); axe.tick_params(labelsize=10.5)
    axe.set_xticks([1, 5, 10])
    axe.set_title(e_note, loc="left", fontsize=12.5)
    amp = np.trapezoid(kern * psi, x, axis=1)
    pd = np.abs(amp)**2 * np.pi                             # density per unit of p / (pi hbar / L)
    axp.fill_between(p, pd, color=ORANGE, alpha=0.25, lw=0); axp.plot(p, pd, color=ORANGE, lw=2.2)
    for sgn in (-5, 5):
        axp.axvline(sgn, color=GRAY, lw=1, ls="--")
    axp.set_xlim(-10, 10); axp.set_ylim(0, 1.25 * pd.max()); axp.set_yticks([]); axp.spines["left"].set_visible(False)
    axp.set_xticks([-10, -5, 0, 5, 10]); axp.tick_params(labelsize=10.5)
    axp.set_title(p_note, loc="left", fontsize=12.5)
axs[1, 0].plot([], [], color=CARDINAL, lw=1.4, label=r"$|\psi|^2$")
axs[1, 0].legend(loc="upper left", frameon=False, fontsize=11, handlelength=1.4, borderaxespad=0.1)
axs[1, 0].set_xlabel(r"position $x$", fontsize=11.5)
axs[1, 1].set_xlabel(r"level $n$  ($E_n = n^2E_1$)", fontsize=11.5)
axs[1, 2].set_xlabel(r"momentum $p$  (units of $\pi\hbar/L$)", fontsize=11.5)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.02, right=0.99, top=0.93, bottom=0.11)
plt.show()

Fig. Two states in a box, each with its energy and momentum readings. Top: the box state ψ5\psi_5ψ5​ gives one energy, 25E125E_125E1​, every time. Its momentum readings fall in two humps near p=±2mE5=±5πℏ/Lp = \pm\sqrt{2mE_5} = \pm 5\pi\hbar/Lp=±2mE5​​=±5πℏ/L (dashed), because the sine is half a wave moving right and half moving left, sin⁡kx=(eikx−e−ikx)/2i\sin kx = (e^{ikx} - e^{-ikx})/2isinkx=(eikx−e−ikx)/2i; the walls cut the wave off after a length LLL, which broadens each hump by about h/Lh/Lh/L. Bottom: a Gaussian packet moving right at about the same speed. Its momentum readings form one hump on the positive side, but its energy readings spread over several levels. Neither state is sharp in both.

The uncertainty principle¶

  • How much spread the commutator forces is the uncertainty principle, the general form of the relation met in Chapter 1:

Uncertainty principle
σA σB≥12 ∣⟨[A^,B^]⟩∣⟹σx σp≥ℏ2\sigma_A\,\sigma_B \geq \frac{1}{2}\,\Big\lvert\big\langle[\hat{A},\hat{B}]\big\rangle\Big\rvert \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \sigma_x\,\sigma_p \geq \frac{\hbar}{2}σA​σB​≥21​∣∣​⟨[A^,B^]⟩∣∣​⟹σx​σp​≥2ℏ​
(19)

  • For position and momentum the commutator is the constant iℏi\hbariℏ, so its average is iℏi\hbariℏ in every state, and the bound ℏ/2\hbar/2ℏ/2 is the same for every state. Squeezing the position spread widens the momentum spread:

Source
# synced: uncertainty_tradeoff
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation
from IPython.display import HTML

TEAL, CARDINAL, GRAY, PURPLE, ORANGE = "#107895", "#C8102E", "#6c757d", "#6a3d9a", "#e07b00"
plt.rcParams.update({"axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})
nf = 40
sx = np.exp(np.log(1.4) + (np.log(0.3) - np.log(1.4)) * 0.5 * (1 - np.cos(2 * np.pi * np.arange(nf) / nf)))
x = np.linspace(-4, 4, 500)                                 # hbar = 1
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(9, 3.4))
gs = fig.add_gridspec(1, 3, width_ratios=[1, 1, 1.05], wspace=0.35)
axx, axp, axu = (fig.add_subplot(gs[0, j]) for j in range(3))
(lx,) = axx.plot([], [], color=TEAL, lw=2.4); bx = [axx.fill_between(x, 0 * x, color=TEAL, alpha=0.2, lw=0)]
(lp,) = axp.plot([], [], color=CARDINAL, lw=2.4); bp = [axp.fill_between(x, 0 * x, color=CARDINAL, alpha=0.2, lw=0)]
for ax, lab in ((axx, r"position $x$"), (axp, r"momentum $p$")):
    ax.set_xlim(-4, 4); ax.set_ylim(0, 1.45); ax.set_yticks([]); ax.spines["left"].set_visible(False)
    ax.set_xlabel(lab, fontsize=12); ax.tick_params(labelsize=10.5)
dx = np.geomspace(0.08, 3, 200)
axu.fill_between(dx, 0.04, 0.5 / dx, color=GRAY, alpha=0.25, lw=0)
axu.plot(dx, 0.5 / dx, color="k", lw=1.6)
axu.plot(dx, 0.568 / dx, color=PURPLE, lw=1.4, ls="--")
axu.text(0.1, 0.35, "forbidden:\n" + r"$\sigma_x\sigma_p < \hbar/2$", fontsize=11, color=GRAY, va="bottom")
(gdot,) = axu.plot([], [], "o", color=TEAL, ms=10, zorder=5, label=r"Gaussian: $\sigma_x\sigma_p = 0.50\,\hbar$")
(bdot,) = axu.plot([], [], "s", color=PURPLE, ms=9, zorder=5, label=r"box ground state: $0.57\,\hbar$")
axu.set_xscale("log"); axu.set_yscale("log"); axu.set_xlim(0.08, 3); axu.set_ylim(0.04, 12)
axu.set_xlabel(r"$\sigma_x$", fontsize=12); axu.set_ylabel(r"$\sigma_p$", fontsize=12); axu.tick_params(labelsize=10)
axu.legend(loc="upper right", frameon=False, fontsize=10.5, handletextpad=0.3, borderaxespad=0.1)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.02, right=0.98, top=0.86, bottom=0.17)

def update(i):
    s = sx[i]; sp = 0.5 / s
    rx = np.exp(-x**2 / (2 * s**2)) / np.sqrt(2 * np.pi * s**2)
    rp = np.exp(-x**2 / (2 * sp**2)) / np.sqrt(2 * np.pi * sp**2)
    lx.set_data(x, rx); bx[0].remove(); bx[0] = axx.fill_between(x, rx, color=TEAL, alpha=0.2, lw=0)
    lp.set_data(x, rp); bp[0].remove(); bp[0] = axp.fill_between(x, rp, color=CARDINAL, alpha=0.2, lw=0)
    axx.set_title(rf"$|\psi(x)|^2$:  $\sigma_x = {s:.2f}$", loc="left", fontsize=12.5)
    axp.set_title(rf"$|\phi(p)|^2$:  $\sigma_p = {sp:.2f}$", loc="left", fontsize=12.5)
    gdot.set_data([s], [sp]); bdot.set_data([s], [0.568 / s])
    axu.set_title(rf"$\sigma_x\sigma_p = {s * sp:.2f}\,\hbar$", loc="left", fontsize=12.5)

ani = FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=nf, interval=120, blit=False)
plt.close(fig)
HTML(ani.to_jshtml())

Fig. A Gaussian squeezed and released. Left: the position distribution. Middle: the momentum distribution, which widens as the position narrows. Right: the two spreads on log axes. The gray region below σxσp=ℏ/2\sigma_x\sigma_p = \hbar/2σx​σp​=ℏ/2 is forbidden. The Gaussian rides exactly on the boundary, the least uncertain state possible; the ground state of a box of matching size (square) sits a little above it, at 0.57 ℏ0.57\,\hbar0.57ℏ.

Example: how uncertain is the box ground state?

For ψ1=2/L sin⁡(πx/L)\psi_1 = \sqrt{2/L}\,\sin(\pi x/L)ψ1​=2/L​sin(πx/L): the average position is L/2L/2L/2 by symmetry, and ⟨x2⟩=L2(13−12π2)\langle x^2\rangle = L^2\big(\tfrac{1}{3} - \tfrac{1}{2\pi^2}\big)⟨x2⟩=L2(31​−2π21​), so

σx=L112−12π2=0.181 L\sigma_x = L\sqrt{\frac{1}{12} - \frac{1}{2\pi^2}} = 0.181\,Lσx​=L121​−2π21​​=0.181L
(20)

The average momentum is zero, and ⟨p2⟩=2mE1=(πℏ/L)2\langle p^2\rangle = 2mE_1 = (\pi\hbar/L)^2⟨p2⟩=2mE1​=(πℏ/L)2, so σp=πℏ/L\sigma_p = \pi\hbar/Lσp​=πℏ/L. The product

σx σp=0.181 π ℏ=0.568 ℏ≥0.5 ℏ\sigma_x\,\sigma_p = 0.181\,\pi\,\hbar = 0.568\,\hbar \geq 0.5\,\hbarσx​σp​=0.181πℏ=0.568ℏ≥0.5ℏ
(21)

does not depend on LLL: a smaller box localizes the particle better and raises its momentum spread by the same factor. This is also why confinement costs energy. Squeezing the box raises σp\sigma_pσp​, and the kinetic energy ⟨p2⟩/2m\langle p^2\rangle/2m⟨p2⟩/2m grows as 1/L21/L^21/L2.

Problems¶

Problem 1: Complex coefficients¶

A particle in a box is in the state ψ=12(ψ1+i ψ2)\psi = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\big(\psi_1 + i\,\psi_2\big)ψ=2​1​(ψ1​+iψ2​). What energies can be measured, with what probabilities? Find ⟨E⟩\langle E\rangle⟨E⟩ and σE\sigma_EσE​.

Solution

The probabilities are the squared magnitudes, ∣1/2∣2=∣i/2∣2=12\lvert 1/\sqrt{2}\rvert^2 = \lvert i/\sqrt{2}\rvert^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}∣1/2​∣2=∣i/2​∣2=21​: half the readings give E1E_1E1​, half give 4E14E_14E1​. The factor iii does not change them. Then

⟨E⟩=12E1+12⋅4E1=2.5 E1,⟨E2⟩=12E12+12⋅16E12=8.5 E12\langle E\rangle = \tfrac{1}{2}E_1 + \tfrac{1}{2}\cdot4E_1 = 2.5\,E_1, \qquad \langle E^2\rangle = \tfrac{1}{2}E_1^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}\cdot16E_1^2 = 8.5\,E_1^2⟨E⟩=21​E1​+21​⋅4E1​=2.5E1​,⟨E2⟩=21​E12​+21​⋅16E12​=8.5E12​
(22)
σE=8.5−6.25  E1=1.5 E1\sigma_E = \sqrt{8.5 - 6.25}\;E_1 = 1.5\,E_1σE​=8.5−6.25​E1​=1.5E1​
(23)

The iii is not invisible to every measurement. It changes where the particle is likely to be found (compare Problem 8), and it changes how the state moves in time.

Problem 2: Averages of observables are real¶

Show that ⟨A⟩=⟨ψ∣A^∣ψ⟩\langle A\rangle = \langle \psi \vert \hat{A} \vert \psi \rangle⟨A⟩=⟨ψ∣A^∣ψ⟩ is a real number whenever A^\hat{A}A^ is Hermitian, for every state ψ\psiψ.

Solution

Take the complex conjugate and use ⟨f∣g⟩∗=⟨g∣f⟩\langle f \vert g\rangle^* = \langle g \vert f\rangle⟨f∣g⟩∗=⟨g∣f⟩, then the Hermitian property:

⟨A⟩∗=⟨ψ∣A^ψ⟩∗=⟨A^ψ∣ψ⟩=⟨ψ∣A^ψ⟩=⟨A⟩\langle A\rangle^* = \langle \psi \vert \hat{A}\psi \rangle^* = \langle \hat{A}\psi \vert \psi \rangle = \langle \psi \vert \hat{A}\psi \rangle = \langle A\rangle⟨A⟩∗=⟨ψ∣A^ψ⟩∗=⟨A^ψ∣ψ⟩=⟨ψ∣A^ψ⟩=⟨A⟩
(24)

A number equal to its own conjugate is real. The expansion gives the same conclusion: ⟨A⟩=∑npnan\langle A\rangle = \sum_n p_n a_n⟨A⟩=∑n​pn​an​ is a sum of real eigenvalues with positive weights.

Problem 3: Two measurements in a row¶

A particle in a box is in the state ψ=12(3 ψ1+ψ2)\psi = \frac{1}{2}\big(\sqrt{3}\,\psi_1 + \psi_2\big)ψ=21​(3​ψ1​+ψ2​). (a) What is the probability that an energy measurement gives E1E_1E1​? (b) The reading is in fact 4E14E_14E1​. What is the state right after, and what does a second energy measurement give? (c) Next the position is measured. Where is the particle never found?

Solution

(a) ∣3/2∣2=34\lvert\sqrt{3}/2\rvert^2 = \tfrac{3}{4}∣3​/2∣2=43​.

(b) The reading 4E14E_14E1​ leaves the particle in ψ2\psi_2ψ2​. A second energy measurement returns 4E14E_14E1​ with probability one: ψ2\psi_2ψ2​ is an eigenfunction of H^\hat{H}H^.

(c) The position distribution is now ∣ψ2(x)∣2=2Lsin⁡2(2πx/L)\lvert\psi_2(x)\rvert^2 = \frac{2}{L}\sin^2(2\pi x/L)∣ψ2​(x)∣2=L2​sin2(2πx/L), which vanishes at the node x=L/2x = L/2x=L/2 (and at the walls). Before the energy measurement the distribution was ∣ψ∣2\lvert\psi\rvert^2∣ψ∣2, which does not vanish at the center: the first measurement changed what the second one sees.

Problem 4: The spread of the parabola¶

For the parabola ψ=30/L5 x(L−x)\psi = \sqrt{30/L^5}\,x(L-x)ψ=30/L5​x(L−x) of the worked example, 99.86 percent of the energy readings give exactly E1E_1E1​. Find σE\sigma_EσE​, using ∑n odd1/n2=π2/8\sum_{n\ \text{odd}} 1/n^2 = \pi^2/8∑n odd​1/n2=π2/8 and ∑n odd1/n4=π4/96\sum_{n\ \text{odd}} 1/n^4 = \pi^4/96∑n odd​1/n4=π4/96.

Problem 5: Expanding a tent¶

Normalize it, then find its expansion coefficients in box states, either by integrating by parts or numerically with the grid code above. What is the probability of measuring E1E_1E1​? How many states hold 99.9 percent of the probability? Compare with the parabola, and explain the difference using the sharp corner of the tent.
